chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Harun ibn Muslim, from Mas'ada ibn Sadaqa, who said:

It was said to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), 'The people are reporting that Ali (peace be upon him) said upon the pulpit of Kufa: O people! You will be called to insult me, so insult me. Then you will be called to disavow me, so do not disavow me.' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'How often do the people lie against Ali (peace be upon him).'

Then he (peace be upon him) said: 'He only said: You will be called to insult me, so insult me. Then you will be called to disavow me, and I am upon the religion of Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family), but he did not say: Do not disavow me.'

So the questioner said to him (peace be upon him), 'What do you think if he chose death rather than disavowal?' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'By Allah! That would not be upon him, and he would have no excuse except what was for 'Ammar ibn Yasir, when the people of Mecca coerced him while his heart was at rest with faith.'
Except the one who is compelled while his heart is at rest with faith.

So the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said to him at that time: O 'Ammar! If they return (to coercing you), so return (to saying what you said), for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has revealed your excuse and commanded you to return if they return.

key_terms.عَمَّارُ بْنُ يَاسِر: Ammar ibn Yasir, a companion known for his dissimulation
key_terms.مُطْمَئِنّ: At rest or firm (regarding the heart)

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Ali (peace be upon him) actually say about being insulted and disavowed, and what is the ruling on dissimulation (taqiyya) in cases of coercion?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) corrects the popular narration by clarifying that he affirmed his adherence to the Prophet's religion rather than commanding public disavowal, thereby distinguishing between the act of *taqiyya* and the internal state of faith. He anchors this ruling in the precedent of 'Ammar ibn Yasir, whose heart remained firm during coercion, establishing the principle that external utterance under duress does not negate inner belief. This hadith serves as a foundational text for Shia jurisprudence on *taqiyya*, emphasizing that the preservation of life through dissimulation is a divine concession, as confirmed by the Prophet's instruction to 'Ammar to repeat the act if persecution continued.
